utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Do you hear me well, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you well, Mr. President, and I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Galic.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind both of us that we should wait for the interpretation to finish. General, how did the 1st Corps of the BH Army honour the zone of total exclusion that had been agreed in the very centre of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement reached on the 18th of February, 1994, is about the exclusion of heavy weapons within 20 kilometres from the centre of Sarajevo. According to the information I had at the time, the 1st Corps of the BH Army did not honour the agreement. I had sufficient information about their activity to draw that conclusion. I pointed that out to all UNPROFOR representatives. I showed them that it didn't apply in the same manner as the withdrawal of my forces from Igman and Bjelasnica, which positions they handed over to the BH Army. But they said that they hadn't done that, but later on it was obvious that they had. I don't know which measures they were taking to have the other side honour the agreement, but basically the 1st Corps of the BH Army according to the information I had did not honour the agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01784, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We are not getting the interpretation. Do you hear me? Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you but probably you mean the interpretation into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, paragraph 2 reads that the enemy did not respect the truce and that they opened sniper fire from the Jewish cemetery and Debelo Brdo with fragmentation ammunition, five rifle grenades, and three grenades from hand-held rocket-launchers. Are the places mentioned here within that 20-kilometre exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these places mentioned are in the territory controlled by the First Corps of the BH Army. They are near the centre of Sarajevo, so certainly within the 20-kilometre exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the next paragraph we can see that grenades of -- make-shift grenades, 82 mm calibre, were fired from the direction of the Agricultural Institute, then they shot at a UN plane from a browning and you also add in item 2 that your forces did not respond to enemy actions except in the zones of the Third Sarajevo Infantry Brigade in Rajlovac and Ilijas. These two, Rajlovac and Ilijas, are they central or peripheral city municipalities?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that Sarajevo before 1991 had about 610.000 inhabitants and it had ten municipalities. Rajlovac and Ilijas are on the outer rim like Pale. There is something else I haven't commented upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. But be brief.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important to point out the fire at the UN helicopter with an anti-aircraft machine-gun of 12.7-millimetre calibre. Up to that calibre, weapons were allowed in the exclusion zone, but we're talking about an anti-aircraft machine-gun which is efficient up to a distance of 1500 metres. This is why that fire is very dangerous and can be provocative. That's what I wanted to add, there are a lot of important matters listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position or the interest of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps with regard to the safety of UN planes and planes carrying humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a number of orders about humanitarian aid. I expected a special chapter of questions about that, so I would be able to say what the obligations of the SRK were with regard to humanitarian aid. Not only the landing of planes at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo because that part was very risky because you had to land between the 1st Corps and the SRK, and we're talking about freight planes here, easy to hit. And whether the fire had been opened from the SRK or the 1st Corps positions is difficult to establish. As far as I know and according to the information I had, we never opened fire at UN planes, not even - if I may add – when Mr. Morillon requested passage to Srebrenica I replied, "I haven’t informed the units because they don't know who's flying above them." And we took measures for him to reach his destination safely. A large amount of risk was involved. Those UN representatives were the one who had to implement what we had ordered, namely, the honouring of all orders with regard to the Geneva Conventions, the protection of civilians, and so on and so forth. Because these are the implementation forces and they should warn both sides of their respective obligations. This is why we respected those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 we read that UNPROFOR accused the Serbian forces as being responsible for yesterday's incident. It -- they point out that the planes were carrying 16 tonnes of fuel and that there was a risk of that plane falling on Ilidza. Was it in our interest for such a plane to fall on the Serb settlement of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if such a plane with 16 tonnes of fuel had crashed in Ilidza, I don't think that much would have remained of Ilidza, I don’t mean just the settlement, but the population that lived there on either side of the frontline. 19 Q. A meeting is scheduled to take place tomorrow between General Galic and General Soubirou, we read here. General Soubirou has proposed the following agenda: A global agreement on anti-sniper action, and then we see that it continues with the free movement and so on and so forth. Did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, yes. There's no confirmation in this report, but Soubirou was the commander of the UNPROFOR sector in which Sarajevo was. He's the person with whom I was supposed to co-operate officially in the zone of responsibility of the SRK. I represented the SRK, and he the UNPROFOR forces and other forces in that area. After the exclusion of heavy weapons in the 20-kilometre zone, we had -- we were in a position where the 1st Corps of the BH Army had a great advantage over the SRK - I had already discussed that so I needn't repeat - and we were all for an anti-sniping agreement because even before all fire from infantry weapons had been called sniping, but this agreement was really only about snipers proper. If you understand it that way, we thought it a good idea to have such an agreement because then the SRK would have been protected and the other day I also mentioned the obligation, or rather, to withdraw heavy weapons from the 20-kilometre zone and how dissatisfied the Serbs were with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last item is number 10. We can't see it in English. A Croat and a Serb crossed the lines and joined you. This person, Mate Gajo Perlind [phoen] is a Croat, right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, he should be. These people who changed sides, there were many of them in 1993 and 1994. They came from the area controlled by the 1st Corps of the BH Army. They were mostly Serbs or Croats but there were also some Muslims. There were -- there were such incidents with people from Sarajevo fleeing across the lines, going from the area controlled by the First Corps of the BH Army to the territory of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. There was an example of a girl and her boyfriend who were killed on a bridge and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a very small thing. At page 3 the witness spoke about an anti-aircraft machine-gun being referred to in the document and the document doesn't say "anti-aircraft machine-gun," so I wonder what he means to describe. There's a weapon in the document called a "Browning," maybe that's the same thing, but just before this is admitted, please, that clarification would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page? Shall we go back to the first page. Could you assist us, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Mr. President. Browning is the name of the weapon. It's a PAM or anti-aircraft machine-gun and the make is Browning. The calibre is 12.7 millimetres. You're right, Madam Prosecutor, it is the same thing, only the word here used is Browning and I called it an anti-aircraft machine-gun because I wanted to explain what a Browning was and how it can be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to sniping and anti-sniping agreements, please explain to the Chamber what a sniper is actually and what kind of sniping units the SRK had and what kind of snipers or sniping rifles and what the purpose was for which the SRK used snipers. What is a sniper actually?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military sense and the civilian sense too, a sniping rifle is a rifle. A gun cannot be called a sniper, although with a gun you also target directly, you fire directly. We had various M-48 rifles of 7.9 millimetre calibre, which apart from a mechanical sight also had an optical sight and that was an optional -- an addition to that rifle and that's what we called a sniping rifle. We had a small number of semi-automatic rifles of 7.62 millimetre calibre which could also be equipped with an optical sight. The optical sight enhances the precision of the rifle which can be used with precision up to 400 metres' distance and the overall range is 800 metres. The bullet of the M-48 7.9 mm rifle can fly as far as 5 kilometres but it can be used with any amount of precision only up to the distances I mentioned. If you equal all infantry weapons with sniping rifles is wrong from the military point of view. I don't know about the legal point of view because you can approach it from various angles. Generals from NATO countries who were here actually agreed with my interpretation and that's the definition widely accepted in the military profession. Apart from optical sights there are also laser sights. You can have equipment for shooting at night and so on. Nowadays there are even more modern weapons and almost any NATO rifle is equipped almost as if it were a sniping rifle. It's not the same with us. So we must distinguish between sniping and other fire from infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to what SRK had, can you just tell us if there are snipers which can fire bursts of fire and what is the precision with regard to moving targets?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the intention of the sniper is to fire single shots because bursts of fire are imprecise and bursts of fire can never be successful sniper fire. That is why we used the rifle from the Second World War practically with which one could achieve what could be achieved. So that would be that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And moving targets?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moving target can be better hit because in the -- with the optical sights you can count in the speed of the moving target, whether it's a man running or some other item moving, then you can calculate the time which is needed and how many metres he would cross in order to shoot in front of the target so that when the object that is targeted comes along then it collides with the bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any sniper units?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps there were no sniper units, no sniper units. There were single sharpshooters, but few. I don't even know how many we had in our corps in total, but not so many. They were assigned across various units and in lower units down to the level of company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was their task?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main task of the sharpshooters or sniping activity was to fight and counter the enemy sniper activities. Next, they could also be used in order to target important targets in combat; for example, if you notice that there is an officer there then the sniper should target him. It shouldn't be an ordinary soldier firing. Then they could also target the openings of bunkers. If there was fire coming from bunkers and there is an opening, then you would have the required level of precision with the sniper to neutralise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Chamber in view of precision at a distance of 400 metres what were the sections of the Sarajevo front at which you could reach the targets and what were the sections where you could only fire at the lines and what were the ones where you could also fire in-depth?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, could you fire from Vidikovac and up to what distance?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to fire from Vidikovac but the question is what was visible from there. It was mostly from the areas just like they did, down along Miljacka from Grbavica, and they shot at us from Marin Dvor, the faculty of mechanical engineering, and up to the government building towards our forces. Likewise, from the high-rises, even though they were somewhat lower, I mean the high-rises on our side, but our snipers were deployed there and our snipers returned such fire. Then we also returned fire in Dobrinja similarly, but also in Dobrinja we had position that was disadvantageous because the high-rises are almost of the same height. We held a smaller section of Dobrinja but they had the rise at Mojmilo so they could use the area more. However, it was still possible to use sniper and other units, or rather, such equipment, sniping equipment because we didn't have such specific units. And then further, if you need me to go on describing the situation, one could say that in part of the Stup and the Stup overpass we also had that though it was not so pronounced. And in the area of Rajlovac in the direction of Brijesce Brdo and Sokolj, there was no chance of using them because of the significant overtowering of their forces so it wouldn't be efficient. Likewise in Vogosca towards Zuc and Orlic, it wouldn't have been much efficient from those sections. What were the areas that could be partly or occasionally used for such fire? Well, that was the area above, or rather, towards Hresa. But only occasionally. It depended. For example, sometimes they would gain the upper hand in that area, sometimes we would -- that was the area towards Spicaste Stijene as they called it. Spicaste Stijene, as far as I remember, was partly under our control at one point and then it was under their control, and the people who were on the positions there told me that they were at the bottom of Spicaste Stijene rather than up there, so it was possible to shoot from the higher parts. As for other sections such as Hresa and Trebevic, I think that it was impossible. Why? Because the buildings which were in the zone of the 1st Corps of the BH Army actually separated this section of Trebevic and Hresa from Sarajevo so that it was not rational to use any such equipment in that specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you tell us something about the same thing, the units, positions, and the use of sniper fire. You already told us something about that, about the 1st Corps, especially in the part of the city where the lines were close to each other and so were the civilian settlements such as Grbavica and Dobrinja. But did they have any sniper formations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony I have already mentioned quite a lot of information up until now, but I would emphasize the following. In the Marin Dvor area and the other areas facing Grbavica, we know that it was only the Miljacka river that separated the two fronts. On the right bank were the positions of the BH Army and on the left bank were the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps along the Miljacka river. And there were always various provocations and shoot-outs. But on their side - when I say "their side," I always mean the 1st Corps of the BH Army - they had stronger buildings on their side so they had more possibilities to use sniper units. According to the information that I had and that the SRK had, the 1st Corps of the BH Army had sniper units within its composition. I said before that we had information that they had around 500 snipers in Sarajevo, whether it was more or less and whether the number increased, because at the Zrak factory which was under their control they could produce optical sights so they could increase the number of such equipment that they would be using during the war, so I cannot say with definite precision what the number was. What is also well-known were specific groups of selected snipers, that is to say the men who used snipers, who acted from the "Seve," that is to say the larks; to "Laste," which are the swallows. They had specific names, all sorts of names were used. Those sniper groups had double use. They fired against our forces, especially in Grbavica, because this thing about the "Seve" was something that was mentioned during the proceedings against me as well. They said that in Grbavica they would target women in mourning. Why? Because there were both Muslim and Croatian and Serbian women living in Grbavica, but mostly the women who were in mourning dressed in black were at the time were Serbian women. That is why they would target women in mourning. This was an explanation as to why they targeted them. At least that is what I understood at the time. Sniper fire in Grbavica was very pronounced. I think I told you how we protected ourselves from the snipers. We would use tents that would be spread across the streets, tacked on one side and the other, that would be a sort of screen protecting from their sniper fire. It was successful only to a degree, but it was better with such a protection than without it. I think that is sufficient about Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you the following. Can you please tell the Chamber how come that the Serbian women used to wear mourning at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many Serbs were killed in this period and elderly Serbian women very often wear black clothes; that is to say, that they are in mourning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in connection with the deaths, what's the connection with mourning?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know our customs, if someone gets killed, whether it's a close relative or not such a close one, then at least for half a year, at least, you're supposed to be in mourning. Women wear it, sometimes men too, not so much but for women it's almost obligatory. At least six months. And some women, especially the elderly women, if they mourn for longer periods they may continue to be in mourning for the rest of their lives because they mourn someone, a son or a husband or somebody else. That is why this was marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the previous document we saw that there were two persons who had crossed over, one Serb and one Croat. Could you learn anything from the people who crossed over about the fire directed at us and the fire directed against their own people that was sometimes used in the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to say another thing here. We already presented something in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, a passage that I gave to soldiers, officers and non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, just a second. Probably it's better for you to repeat your answer kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Was I too fast or -- yes, too fast. I would like to ask the question to be formulated again briefly and then it will be easier for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was that we could have seen from the previous document there were two men who crossed over in one single day, one Serb and one Croat. Did you receive any specific information from those who crossed over, specifically with regard to the fire of Muslim snipers especially against their own territory and their own civilians?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the persons who crossed over, sometimes they were fewer, sometimes they were more numerous, but it could be up to 15 people in a single day who crossed over from the territory under the control of the BH Army to the territory under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And they were quite a significant source of information for us about the situation in the territory under the control of the 1st Corps of the BH Army because they had to experience everything that was going on there, and they knew what were the measures taken against them in the territory under the control of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, especially in camps and other places where they were detained, how they were treated, and so on and so forth. And of course we would later forward this information to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and likewise we received information about the deployment of the forces and equipment of the 1st Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Starting with Marin Dvor and then downstream, could you tell us what were the buildings or facilities where snipers' nests were deployed on the Muslim side? You can start from Momo and Uzeir the two Unis high-rises and then further on.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would rather tell you what were the general things that I could notice and then mention specific buildings because there were too many. All the buildings with reinforced concrete that were higher than three floors were used for sniper fire. From parts of their deployment in Marin Dvor, the faculty of mechanical engineering, and down to Dobrinja, the territory that was under the control of the BH Army. Then from Alipasino Polje, the students' halls of residence, Stupska Petlja overpass, and along the entire front practically because we know what were the other dominant features such as Sokolja Dol [phoen], Zuca, and on the opposite side up to Grdonj and Debelo Brdo facing Grbavica. So I think I have now closed the circle, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what sort of orders did you issue? Did you issue orders to open sniper fire against targets that were not legitimate, on civilians, and so on? What sort of orders did you issue with regard to this? You and your subordinates, at least as far as you knew.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for sniper fire, the fire of various snipers, I said that we did not have sniper units. So the level of command and control which could issue such tasks directly were platoon commanders at the highest and occasionally company commanders. The higher levels of command and control did not deal with such issues except in extraordinary circumstances. My orders were never such that the targets could include civilians. My orders also said that no one was entitled and did not have the right to target a civilian or select civilians as targets. So when selecting a target, everyone would have to decide to select military targets. Now, whether there was fire that was not in accordance with this and whether there was too much or disproportionate fire at some points, I believe we'll talk about that soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you receive information, through reports or protests? What did you receive about sniper fire and to what extent were such reports accurate?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for protests about sniper fire, we did discuss here some protests that I responded to. Essentially, there was a general protest with regard to such fire, so they would say: Such and such a place was targeted by sniper fire, but on the basis of this you could not take any measures. There were no direct protests in connection with sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were no specific protests?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, what I know today, what you know today, what the Court knows today, I didn't know that at the time, that somebody got killed from sniping fire. How was I supposed to know that? I did not receive such information and I could not react because there was no information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Our soldiers, our shooters, could they distinguish between Muslim and Serbian civilians in the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far that was not said during my trial and I've not mentioned that during my testimony here. I would like to say in Sarajevo on the territory of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army, according to what we know some 30.000 Serbs remained living in the area, 15.000 families times two family members amounted to 30.000 Serbs. Their situation was very difficult. They lived in 40 camps in and outside of Sarajevo from Silos to the central prison. As for distinction being made between a civilian Serb and a civilian Muslim, I don't think that a soldier on the front line could make that distinction at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the indictment against me, there are allegations about an alleged 14 sniping incident whereby a 3-year-old child was wounded in the right leg on a porch 15 or balcony of its house in Zagrici street, Sirokaca area, on the 13 December 1992. 16 I believe that the location from which that fire was open was pin-pointed as 17 Stijene Baba. Did you issue that order? Did you receive report about that incident?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the area of Sirokaca. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sirokaca. From Stijene Baba to Sirokaca.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With hindsight when I tried to remember all those incidents that we have discussed so far - and you have to know that during my trial we discussed a total of 37 such incidents - it's very difficult to remember each and every one of them, but I do remember the one that you have just mentioned now. That area, Baba Stijene, was not entirely… was below the road which leads from Lukavica to Pale. One part was… they may have had access, the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The remaining part below… immediately below the road there were positions of the BiH Army. In that area where Pita was wounded, I apologise, if I’m mistaken, but that was 20 years ago and my memory has faded, but you jogged my memory during the prepping. I hope I said it right, if not, I apologise. That girl was injured when she returned and one needs to mention that over there there were positions and trenches of the BiH Army close to her house and that troops were moving around probably going as a replacement to the positions at Sirokaca. Whether any of the soldiers were there at the moment when she got hit would be mere speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some troops passing by her house headed towards the positions, as a replacement, whose troops?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the BiH army, the 10th Mountain Brigade was deployed there in the area for a while and later on it was 105th Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 115th?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends, it could have been both. I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D6308.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your report which was issued on the 13th of December, 1992, when that incident happened. Could you please tell me this: Did you issue the order for sniping fire to be opened on that girl or did any of your subordinates order that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the report in front of me, but my eyes can't see it. It's -- the letters are too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you please first answer my question about the order. Who ordered it? Whether an order was issued? Did you receive information that somebody else had issued the order?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For somebody to order that fire should be opened on a child or a civilian in general, honestly I never heard that any such order was issued in my corps. I'm sure that I never issued such an order. Nobody who commanded me ordered any such thing. It's absolutely inconceivable that anybody could have issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at your report and can you see what your report at 1800 hours contained. There is a reference to battles in the Rajlovac and Vogosca Brigades. The enemy artillery fired at Blazuj, Nedzarici, Grbavica, and Mrkovici, and so on and so forth, and it also says that our artillery opened fire on the enemy artillery positions. There is no reference to any activities in Sirokaca. What can you tell us about that? If there had been fire opened on Sirokaca, would you have omitted that from your report?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to 13 December 1992, right, that's the date that you're asking me about. At that time fighting was still going on for Otes. At that time the BiH army put a lot of pressure on Zuc. Fierce fighting was ongoing in that area. Sirokaca is on the other side of the front line and there should not have been any major activity in that area at the time. Major activities started taking place sometime around the 20th of December when the forces should have been linked up in the final stages of Jug 92 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked you this: If there had been any activities in Sirokaca, would that have been reported to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there had been activities and if we had received information from our subordinated units that something of that kind had happened in that area, I'm sure that we would have reported back to the Main Staff because Sirokaca was a sensitive area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D01486. Can the document be zoomed in for the benefit of the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was issued on the 26th of February, 1993. You reported, in the first item, about sniping fire and fire being open on the Rajlovac barracks from Sokolje and under item i.-- on other locat...—- on Grbavica, and under 7 you can see the effects of the sniping activity in Grbavica. One civilian was killed by sniper fire and a number of civilians were wounded. To -- what was the ratio between civilians and soldiers who were wounded in Grbavica? Who were the most commonplace casualties?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I remember the information that we had at that time, there were a lot of wounded and killed civilians in Grbavica. The percentage or the ratio between civilians and soldiers must have been or I assume that it was 1:2, but in any case there were more wounded and dead civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D01519. If the document is blown up a little, the General will be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your report for the 29th of March, 1993, at 1800 hours. 8 You reported that during the cease-fire agreement which is not being observed by the enemy, there was a sniping fire open on -- from Sokolje on Dvor, from Mojmilo on Lukavica, from Dobrinja 1 against the airport settlement, and under item 2 you say that the SRK units generally are adhering to the cease-fire agreement and do not respond to the enemy provocations. Towards the end of the document under 7 you say: "Casualties: One soldier in Ilidza was killed." Does that mean that in the other locations where fire was opened there were no casualties? What was the reason why you did not return fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says in the report that only one soldier was killed, that was based on the information that I had at the time, so I cannot base my report on the information that I may have obtained in the meantime. A cease-fire was in effect at the time and we could not respond but you see that I'm -- mentioned all the places from which sniper fire was opened and that's precisely where it was opened from, where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can also see that there was a meeting dealing with the freedom of movement, but why didn't you respond to the enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was the fact that the cease-fire was in effect, as I've already told you, and there were negotiations going on about blue paths or blue roads which would allow civilians to go in and out of the area of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army and the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That would have been two directions that civilians could have taken in order to enter and leave those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3438, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the indictment against me there are allegations about an incident which happened on the 17th of April, 1993. Allegedly a 9-year-old girl was shot at and wounded in the back while she was playing in her own front yard in Sedrenik in Sarajevo. First of all, can you tell us whether you ordered that fire to be opened or whether somebody else ordered that. Did you receive a report on that incident at all?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Sedrenik is linked to the firing around Spicaste Stijene, if I am not mistaken. That girl who was wounded in the back and when –- we did not have that information then, it was not made known to us at all. We did not receive information about that nor did we report about that. I can share what I learned subsequently during my trial, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you or anybody else order to open fire on civilians in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I've already told you, such an order could not have existed. Nobody ordered to -- fire to be opened on civilians. If anybody opened fire that was done unbeknownst to us against any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell the Trial Chamber, starting from Mrkovici above Spicaste Stijene, whose positions were there and how far were the Serb positions away from the settlement known as Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and think of all these positions up there. There was Pavlovic, Pavlovic Kosa, there's Grdonj of course, and there is also the part known as seven forests or seven woods. The part where Spicaste Stijene is located was approximately a kilometre away from Sedrenik or perhaps even a kilometre and a half. I apologise if I'm mistaken. I am talking off the top of my head, but it's very difficult to remember all of the details, but I would very much like to answer all of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between our positions and Sedrenik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You were cut off, Mr. Galic, while you were saying that you wanted to share what you learned subsequently to during your trial. Could you tell us briefly what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question, Your Honour. At the time when I was in command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I did not receive any information about any sniping incidents in Sedrenik. At that time I did not have any information, I did not receive any data so I could not react because I was unaware of any such thing. During my trial that incident was discussed and based on that I can tell you that it had been established that one could not see the area where that girl was from the positions where our troops was. And if you look at the entry/exit wound on that girl you could see that she was lying down when she was shot at or something of that kind. In any case, her location could not be seen from the positions where our troops were deployed at that time. I'm sorry if I don't remember all the details. It was also said during that -- my trial that there were some other troops or trenches in the vicinity of that house. It was only normal when you look at the map of the deployment of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army and if you copied those positions on the map depicting all the incidents that are mentioned, you will see immediately what happened, whether there were any troops in the area. I'm sure that there were, but I can't tell you how many and where they were deployed. I was not in a position to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us see 1D54365, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D54365 -- oh, there is no 3 in there, so ... It's 1D5465 without the number 3. This is it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the date is the 17th of April. General Manojlo Milovanovic, the deputy commander of the Main Staff, is issuing this warning to be alert and raise combat-readiness. There is -- there are the preparations for Easter mentioned here and the recipient is reminded that on Orthodox holidays the enemy mostly attacks Serbian villages. There is a reminder of Kravica and other massacres of civilians. It says ensure maximum alertness, increase the number of patrols, and so on. Here is my question: Did we step-up or step-down our combat activities during our holidays?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During major holidays of ours combat activity was moderate. It wasn't stepped down. We wanted to maintain the status quo, but it certainly was not stepped up at the time. That is why we see here that General Milovanovic in his order demands that about 50 per cent of the manpower be at the positions. The usual case is that two-thirds are at the positions and one-third is resting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The general here says "calmed down" rather than moderate. Does it follow from this order of the Main Staff that combat activity is to be boosted on the occasion of Easter?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the occasion of Easter, combat activity is not boosted but reconnaissance and observation is. Various provocations by the BH Army followed and the general reminded of situations around Srebrenica. There was a massacre in that area at Christmas time, and we also referred to such events. There had been such events in the area of the SRK, but those are mostly about the infiltration of sabotage units that were able to penetrate the lines and return to their territory because the soldiers -- our soldiers were a bit relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid although I speak at a moderate pace my questions are simplified. In line 9 I said the general said that combat activity is calmed down and not moderate, as it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see here that you also received this document, it says "SRK."

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we certainly issued an own order as a follow-up. And sometimes when there was no time to rephrase it, then we also passed on the original order. But we did always draft an own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this was on the 17th of April, that is the day of the alleged incident with that girl at Sedrenik, it was also not entered as part of my question.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the date stated here is the 17th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3439, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've already mentioned that the Muslims had their positions at Spicaste Stijene. Generally speaking, General, did we have positions anywhere without the Muslims having their own positions facing ours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know where the General said what Dr. Karadzic is attributing to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On two pages before this one we'll find it. While we are looking, could the General please answer this question I just put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could one side have its positions without enemy positions facing them?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Sarajevo area there were no such instances, but elsewhere there were large stretches of no man's land that were as wide as a few kilometres sometimes. But in Sarajevo areas without forces were very small, and when there were a need, then there would be a rapid intervention to take that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 10, line 3, is an instance of the General saying that the Muslims had their forces up there. And on page 9, lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see 1D1582. Page 10, line 1 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, were there any forces of theirs between our positions at Trebevic and the Sedrenik development?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were forces of theirs, and I believe that I gave a similar answers to the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a regular combat report for the 28th of August, 1993, the hour is 1700. Under item 1 you immediately say that they violated the cease-fire agreement, and among the places from which they did so we see bullet 2 saying from Spicaste Stijene with rifle grenades on the Mrkovic sector and with an anti-aircraft gun on Donji Biosk. Can you tell us, General, what these places are, Mrkovici and Donji Biosk?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrkovici is a housing development and Donji Biosk is another inhabited neighbourhood. Mrkovici is beyond the Sedrenik area and Spicasta Stijena -- actually, it's a village. When I was saying that they had positions at Spicaste Stijene, it's actually confirmed here in this report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D0158 -- no 524, please. 1D01524.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a report of the 4th of May, 1993, the hour is 1700. You report to the Main Staff about activity directed against Vojkovici with 30-millimetre gun from Igman, four 82 mm shells on the Serbian part of Dobrinja, successfully repelled attack against Perivoje village, it’s the Rajlovac Brigade. Look at item 7 and the losses. Three soldiers killed, four wounded, and one civilian, and the conclusion reads: "In spite of all measures taken, the intensive enemy sniper fire inflicting heavy casualties on us as a result of the relaxed behaviour of soldiers and civilians. Two soldiers were killed and one wounded by sniper fire today." And further down in the decision it says activities towards Ormanje and Igman. Are these two on the outer rim of the area or at the front line?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report covers the major part of the zone of responsibility of the corps. It really summarises what happened in Sarajevo and in the close surroundings. We listed the municipalities belonging to Sarajevo and one of them is Hadzici. About Hadzici and the direction of Pazarici there is mount Ormanje. That part of territory is above Hadzici in the direction of Pazarici. At that time speaking about our activities directed at Ormanje, there was a huge pressure off the population at Hadzici in connection with the events at the silos camp at Tarcin, which is behind Ormanje. According to the information we had at the time, we were able to reach that Silos to see what was going on there. I even issued some equipment and gave some forces to the Igman Brigade commander, but these were not used efficiently and I proposed that that commander be replaced later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, talking about sniping, how do you assess these losses in one day, especially the fact that two soldiers were killed and one was wounded -- or four were wounded plus one civilian due to sniping?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking into consideration all the enemy activities and our own activities to prevent these and launch some attacks outside of Sarajevo, then the losses are slightly higher than average, which is justified in such situations. Of course it's always better to have smaller losses, but this is average more or less under such conditions of active defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01532, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your report to the Main Staff for the 17th of May, 1993. Under item 1 you speak about opening fire from infantry weapons and you single out sniping. So in your reports you distinguish between infantry fire and sniping.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always in favour of sending out such reports. It was popular to say -- no, it wasn't infantry fire. It was sniping. Then it makes a greater impression on the higher command and the media and everybody if you say that -- if you speak about sniping, but we distinguished between these two things because they're different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One woman was wounded here and then under item 2 you speak about stepped-up surveillance and reconnaissance and respect of the agreed cease-fire. Or did you not respond to the wounding of this civilian woman?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 17th of May and we want to honour the order about, or rather, follow the order on the honouring of the cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you're interested, but maybe I should say so now so that we don't go back to the question of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that yet. It says here under forecast: "It is to be expected that enemy provocations will continue with the aim of provoking our fire." Why did they want to provoke our fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the BH Army had both a political and military interest to provoke us. They had already reached their political goals because the NATO forces and other forces had already sided with them. So it only remained to -- for them to provoke NATO to openly side with the BH Army. I'm not sure if I'll interpret this correctly, but General Rose said to me once that he had asked General Delic: How long are we supposed to wage war for you? When they had asked him to do something against the VRS. They were always on the side of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. I'm always limiting myself to that corps - which was very rare when it comes to us. I never asked anybody to side with us; I just wanted them to be fair. They were supposed to point out to both sides how they should wage war, but I don't think they really carried out their assignment completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D01544.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report from you to the Main Staff for the 3rd of June, 1993, and in item 1, line 1, we can see that a truce is in force but that it is violated. We can see the various places where they fired from mortars on Rajlovac, from Lemezi cemetery, mortars on civilian buildings in Ilidza from Hrasnica. And under item 2 you say: "Our units have stepped up reconnaissance and surveillance and they are additionally surveying the positions." That's under item 2 [as interpreted]. And under item 7 you say that two soldiers were wounded by sniper fire, whereas two soldiers were wounded in Ilidza, so a total of four wounded and two women were killed by sniper fire in the Aerodrom settlement, the airport settlement. And further on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just have a correction to the transcript, I suppose, please. And this sort of thing happens when Dr. Karadzic reads out what's actually what we can read in the document, but the transcript on page 30, line 16, says "... from Lemezi cemetery from civilians targets in Hrasnica," and that's not what the document says. The document says enemy mortar fire from the direction of Hrasnica hit civilian targets in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. That's quite correct. Perhaps I tried to sum up what everyone can read, but let me move on to my point immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you respond to this fire where you had four wounded soldiers and two women killed by sniper fire in airport settlement and also there was mortar fire against civilian targets in your area?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at where the losses were sustained or from what direction the fire arrived, if that was the area where they targeted the airport settlement, that's from Dobrinja on the airport settlement, and other fire - let me not repeat what's written in the document - any sort of response in those areas would represent a violation of the truce that was in force and would likewise have probably caused other losses, unnecessary losses of civilians and others. That was why we decided to avoid responding in this specific period and that is the 5th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D01554 is the document we would need now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your report for the 23rd of June, 1993, and under item 1 you say that the enemy is not observing the truce and in line 2 you say that there was firing from infantry weapons and sniper rifles. So here you also make a distinction between infantry fire and sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that it's the section of Grbavica that was under our control where one woman was shot dead. I would turn your attention to that part of the report under item 1, because we distinguished [as interpreted], we always wanted to distinguish, sniper fire from infantry weapons fire even though this is difficult to do, I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can also see that by burning wood on Mount Trebevic they are threatening your positions. And under item 2 observation and reconnaissance is continuing. Then under item 7 this woman is mentioned, one soldier wounded in the barracks. Why didn't you respond to these losses and to these enemy activities, enemy fire from various weapons, in particular the snipers at this point?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a new element here, a new activity on their part and that was burning the bush and burning the wooded areas, bush-like trees in particular because fire would then spread quickly, though that depended on the direction of the wind. We know that the wind may blow down a mountain slope or up the mountain slope. They usually used the moments when the wind was blowing upwards towards Trebevic because it would then spread the fire towards Trebevic, towards our positions and in that way they would achieve to chase away our forces even without any combat. However, the fire did not spread much up the slope as far as I remember, but there was fire. As for the other fire and activities, that was on average like previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why you did not respond?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I always focus on the main section of the document which says that there is a cease-fire or some sort of truce in force and that the wish was to observe the truce. I think that this was the end of a truce that had already been at stake because of the activities of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. In such a situation there was still a wish to try and preserve peace as much as possible. We did not respond because we wanted to observe the truce and in order to avoid unnecessary losses, even though we had quite a few losses as you can see from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you will now order us to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But just before that let me ask you one thing: Before a truce were there legitimate goals and what is a legitimate goal during a truce? Is one allowed to shoot during a truce at all?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if a cease-fire was ordered, most often it was just a cease-fire or a cessation of any firing which meant any fire from any combat hardware or equipment or weapons. And then no firing at any target with any weapon was allowed. That was what it meant. In such situations we stuck to the rule that we would inform the UNPROFOR about the locations from which the truce was being violated and with which weapons, and we would say that we would have to respond if that was repeated for our personal safety or our duty to keep our positions in the defence zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be Exhibit D3444. And before we break, Mr. Robinson, the witness who is going to testify on Wednesday will be testifying viva voce and in public?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I am aware that there's an issue with regard to preparation for that witness that may affect tomorrow's scheduling. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, as Mr. Tieger indicated during our last session last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So tomorrow we'll have the first break for an hour and the lunch break will be half an hour, in conclusion ending up at 3.00. Would it suit the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also the -- given the estimate of the length of the examination-in-chief and Mr. -- it's evident that Mr. Galic should stay over until next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It appears that we haven't had an estimate for cross-examination of General Galic, but it appears unlikely we will be able to complete his testimony this week. I remind the Chamber that next week we have a break, so we would be resuming the week of the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And is the planning that the parties are going to conclude Mr. Akashi's -- Ambassador Akashi's evidence on Wednesday? Then could that continue on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the plan is that Mr. Akashi's evidence would spill over until Thursday and that sometime on Thursday General Galic would resume his testimony completing the rest of that day, and then if we don't finish with him he would have to resume testimony around the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at three past 11.00. Just -- before we break, yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to tell the Chamber that I'm based in Geneva and not in The Hague, and I don't know when I will be able to come back after the 6th of May. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Galic, the Chamber has been informed of your back problem. The Chamber has no difficulty with you standing at any time to ease yourself. And further, please let us know if you need a rest at any time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope that my lawyer will say something more with regard to my health and other issues. I asked him to speak, but if necessary I can say that myself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you like to add anything, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. I think it might be a good idea if General Galic would talk about his problems now for this may affect his testimony and his concentration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to stand up, if I may, because when I address the Chamber I prefer to stand. Thank you. Well, Your Honours, you know that I was injured during my arrest in 1999 and that my spine was damaged as well as my shoulder and my teeth and I had major problems because I could not walk for six months here. The objection to the manner of arrest was rejected. I was operated on in Germany two years ago, they operated my spine, but it was not successful. So I still have my old problems and now new ones as well. During my trip from Germany to the Netherlands, the trip lasted three days. I requested to fly precisely because of my spine problems. Others are something that I can tolerate, but they did not agree to that. I'm not sure who decided on that. I had to be transported in a vehicle. I was isolated the first night, the next night I travelled to Arnhem for the whole night up until 11.00 a.m., then I slept with others, but I couldn't sleep because there were four other men who were smoking and talking, and then it was only on the third day on Friday that I arrived here. I was quite tired and exhausted considering that at the time I had also problems with my denture being made. I had injuries while I was in Germany and maybe you noticed that I had difficulty speaking on the first day here because it was only here that they made the dentures smaller. I had lesions in my mouth and these problems date back to December. So I would ask you if it would be possible for me to fly back or -- as when I returned in 2009 in the direction of Freiburg. In the Detention Unit they have a decent and correct attitude toward me, nothing special. But please, there is no need at all to check on me in my cell every 60 minutes in the night because it affects me. I wake up, I'm a soldier, I still have good reflexes. Even though I am 70-years-old, my reflexes are still quite good, so sometimes they wake me up even though I must admit that the guards are really very sensitive and careful. They cannot be more careful than that, but I would kindly ask you to stop monitoring me. There is no need to monitor me at all because then I could peacefully focus on the trial. That was all, your President. It was a bit long-winded. But that's how things stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galic. The Chamber will take a look into the matter. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, my indictment includes an incident dated 11th of July, 1993. According to the indictment, Munira Zametica lost her life while she was getting water from Dobrinja, in the Dobrinja area. Can you please tell us, first of all, whether you or one of your subordinates ordered such fire and did you receive a report about this incident?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I previously said that such incidents, sniping incidents as they are called here, were something that I did not receive reports about. I don't remember any of the ones which were mentioned during the trials, even during my own trial. This incident when people were fetching water from the Dobrinja river, that was an incident that I learned about during my trial and during the war I was not familiar with it. I was not aware of this incident nor did anyone report me about that. But during my trial we arrived at some conclusions which might throw more light on this incident. At the place where she was taking water from the Dobrinja river, there was a bridge above that location and there were some sacks there, and it was said that the soldiers responded when fire was opened from the territory of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. They said that we fired from the church, the new church behind Dobrinja, the new one that was newly constructed, it was new as far as I know. But it was damaged by recoilless gun-fire from Mojmilo, from the BH Army positions. So in that area up there I never saw any of my soldiers going out there, but they said that that was the area from which the fire came. That is what I remember this incident by if I have described it well and if I describe the circumstances under which it may have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So to return to my question, did you order, did you receive a report that one of your subordinates ordered this, or did you receive an official report about this incident?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could all be answered by one negative, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you knew enough about the presence of the BH Army in Dobrinja and also about their deployment, where were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there is one basic rule in the army and it is this: A commanding officer at one level should be aware of the deployment of forces at two levels down. And as for the remainder of the deployment is up to others. I'm the sixth level or thereabouts, the sixth level of command and control. I was quite well aware of the deployment in Dobrinja and also on the main front line of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which brigade was deployed in Dobrinja, how many troops did it have? What was the density of the troops deployed in that area?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If we look at the area of Dobrinja which is above Mojmilo, Goranovo neighbourhood, in Alipasino Polje and goes towards the Serbian territory, towards Nedzarici and the airport, we will see that the area is not very big. It was held by the 5th Mountain Brigade. According to some estimates, there were about 3.000 troops there. The figure is not accurate. This is just an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the 5th Brigade of the BiH Army, did they have snipers among them?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously during my testimony we said that all of their units had sniper units, not only sniper rifles, but also entire units which were used and they were under the direct command of superior commands. They were not used on the orders of a lower-ranking officer. They were used at the brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D01546.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document to be uploaded, for the record I'd like to state that the Chamber wants to receive a Rule 33 submission from the Registry with respect to General Galic's statement -- submission as soon as practicable. I wonder whether the Prosecution wants to respond to what Mr. Galic stated?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your report to the Main Staff. It was issued on the 7th of June. Please pay attention to bullet point (b) where it says in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade where sniper fire was opened on Grbavica as well as on the Lukavica-Bijelo Polje road from Dobrinja 1, 2, and 3. Who held Dobrinja 1, 2, and 3 settlements?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not live in Sarajevo, I cannot be very precise when it comes to roads or particular neighbourhoods. I apologise to the Trial Chamber and all of those who are listening to my evidence. However, as far as I know from documents, that area, area 1, 2, and 3 were held by the 1st Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? Can the English page be scrolled up, please. Well, no, we need the second page or the next page. Let's also look at the second page in Serbian. Let's see sniper fire from Dobrinja. I'm interested in C5. It says here in the third paragraph from the top: Today in the afternoon, sniper fire intensified from the direction of Dobrinja, quadrant C5. This is enemy fire; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is enemy fire and fire was opened on one part of Dobrinja which was under the control of the 5th Mountain Brigade of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up a document that has already been admitted, it's D3418 dated the 11th July, on the same day when the incident involving the late Munira Zametica happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at what was reported at 1700 hours on the 11th of July. It says here that the enemy opened fire along most of the corps defence line. And under 2 it says our forces are reinforcing their position. And then it says there were no other incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Serbian page be scrolled up in order to display bullet point 4. That's the last line. There were no other incidents. Can we go to the following page in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see here that Savo Kuljanin was killed and that Milenko Urta was seriously injured. Could you tell us why this incident involving Munira Zametica was omitted from this daily report?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at the date when all of that was going on and if you look at the rest of the text you will see that that was while Lukavac 93 operation was ongoing. That means that that part of the Sarajevo front line, that was the south-western part of the front line, was under fire on both sides. All the troops there were engaged. At that time we did not report on Mrs. Zametica because we were not aware of that incident. Therefore, my people at the command post could not report about that. This was signed by Milosevic. In that time I was in a different position, I was observing and commanding Lukavac 93 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that provocative fire was being opened on all separation lines. How far is Lukavac 93 front line from the place of the incident in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to be aware of the situation you have to know that the airport is an obstacle. On the one side there is Dobrinja where the incident involving sniper fire happened and on the other side of the airport towards Hadzici and Mount Igman is the area where that operation was taking place and it spilled over towards Trnovo and Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D01572.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report sent by your command to the Main Staff on the 2nd of August on St. Ilija's [phoen] day in 1993. Again it says here that the cease-fire was not observed and that sniper fire was opened from Dobrinja 5 from Stupska Petlja. It is also said that from the Hasici houses sector three shells were fired towards UNPROFOR in Skenderija and another shell was repeated. What is the purpose of that fire being opened by the Muslim forces on UNPROFOR? Judging by the name, when you see this location, Hasici houses, who did those houses belong to, by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to understand one thing, it's very difficult to look at any of the front lines in the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in isolation, is it only in the urban or in the suburban area. You have to bear in mind a whole; however, at that time we were already very deep behind the lines. They needed to provoke NATO hoping that NATO would prevent further advancement of the VRS. That's why they were provoking UNPROFOR. They wanted to blame the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, i.e., the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain the Trial Chamber when it comes to this cease-fire what part of the front line did that apply to in view of the operation on Mount Igman and Lukavac 93 and violations of the cease-fire in the city? Was that a regional cease-fire or was it applied across the board in all of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Two things. Perhaps Dr. Karadzic can take another try at phrasing that question. And at page 42, line 19, it's not Hadzici sector, it's Hasica Kuca, and that could probably have been avoided if Dr. Karadzic slowed down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. Indeed I did mention Hasica Kuca and not Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You never answered that question. In terms of ethnicity, whose houses were those?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the name of the location, ethnic groups can be distinguished by family names but not all. Sometimes different ethnic groups share the same family name. However, Hasici should be a Muslim name. I believe that I know approximately where those houses are, but I can't be sure so I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What types of cease-fires existed in terms of the regional outlay of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did that cease-fire apply to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for putting this question to me. I'm very happy that you did. What happened here was a very controversial account of the situation that had been arrived at. You can see very clear that in the urban area of Sarajevo, in the centre of Sarajevo, there should have been a cease-fire in place. That was an order.
