As far as I can remember -- or rather, I can't remember that order because I was at a forward command post, and at that time the forward command post in question was somewhere at the foot of Mount Bjelasnica. I'm sure that the order applied only to the urban area of Sarajevo. That's where a cease-fire should have been in place. I myself did not receive such an order. I was ordered to proceed, to carry on until the 11th of August. I believe that was the situation, that I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On line 10 it should read: "I did not receive such a cease-fire order to be implemented so far from the urban area of Sarajevo." Is that correct, General? Just the contrary what -- was the case, you received an order to carry on your combat activities?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very precise and I can't tell you where I was on the 2nd of August, but as far as I can remember it was at the foot of Mount Bjelasnica in one of the villages there. That was very far from Sarajevo, some 27 kilometres away from Sarajevo. In that area I did not receive an order to cease fire. Just the contrary was the case. I was ordered to carry on. I'm sure that that was the case. I was in charge of that axis and I know for a fact that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under 2 it says that you should not respond.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Conclusions and forecasts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need that in English as well. Perhaps it's on the last page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here that enemy provocations can be expected to continue along with firing on our positions and at UNPROFOR forces so as to blame our forces and bring about foreign military intervention. SRK units are to keep strictly to the ordered cease-fire measures and they shall fire only with the permission of the higher command when directly threatened. Can you tell us briefly what this means?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those forces which were in Sarajevo itself had to observe the cease-fire and they will respond only if necessary. I can repeat what that means.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just one thing for the record, Dr. Karadzic has been good about clarifying this, but he forgot to mention this is not the General's document, it's General Milosevic's document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the General was able to explain who was authorised to sign. This is from the corps command so he said who was authorised in the commander's stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat, General, who was authorised to sign such documents?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The advisors and the deputies of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see 1D01575. 1D01575.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 8th of August. It says a cease-fire agreement is still not honoured. Kula was fired at from PAMs from Dobrinja 1 and Mujezinovica houses. Our units did not return fire. And then you were exposed to 82-millimetre mortar fire at Gornji Kotorac. And then at Lukavica road rifle grenades and two 82-millimetre shells at Traparine houses, infantry fire and sniping and so on from 8 Sokolovic Kolonija, Dobrinja 3 and 5. The corps units are engaged in reconnaissance 9 and observation but did not respond to the provocations and activity of the enemy. What was the reason for that restraint?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said earlier that there was a cease-fire of that -- in that part of town in force for both sides. However, we see that the enemy side, that is, the 1st Corps of the BH Army, does not honour the agreement and the forces of the SRK along that part of the front line are honouring it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please explain. It says here infantry fire and sniper fire from these localities. Where are they? Stupsko Brdo, Butmir, Vojnicko field, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Dobrinja 3 and 5.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed in this order then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it in town or outside town and where are they with respect to the airport?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinja and the others are in town, whereas Sokolovic Kolonija are beyond the airport toward the Igman mountain. And Dobrinja and the other town part are in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Vojnicko field and Butmir --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Butmir is toward Igman further away from the airport, whereas Vojnicko field is near Alipasino Polje, so between Dobrinja and Alipasino Polje there is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe the Trial Chamber knows the area. Perhaps they have also visited the locations.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I hope that I was able to explain well enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the indictment against me there is another incident dated the 3rd of September, 1993, Nafa Taric and her 8-year-old daughter Elma were wounded with one bullet at the Ivana Krndelj Street in the centre of Sarajevo. The bullet hit the left thigh of the mother and the right hand and belly of the girl, but I don't want to ask you about these ballistic things which are very complicated, but let me know whether you know of this incident or whether you ordered fire or one of your subordinates, and did you have the information that this happened on the 3rd of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This incident as well as nearly all incidents of sniper fire, as stated in the indictment, the question is always whether it was really sniper fire. But I didn't order this or any other activity direct against this area. Perhaps there was activity launched in reaction to enemy activity, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see now how you informed the Main Staff -- let us see 65 ter 12386. 65 ter 12386.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we are waiting let me say that in this area there were shelters in protection against infantry fire. It's surprising that anyone may have been hit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this should be translated as "shelter." Possibly a different translation would be better. You mean obstacles?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can be mobile or stationary. I think it was UNPROFOR that did something and it was in this sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How are you reporting to the Main Staff on that day at 1700 hours: "The enemy did not observe the cease-fire agreement and opened fire ..." and so on. The third paragraph: "In the Sanac, Grbavica sector, the enemy opened intensive small arms fire and during the day they opened sniper fire on the barracks..." and so on. On the 3rd of September there is no mention of this alleged fire directed at Ivana Krndelj Street.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the following page in both languages. We're interested in item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that there were no unusual incidents. Subsequently we see that Captain first class commander -- company commander Radomir Stojanovic was killed on Grbavica by sniper fire from the direction of Hrasno P Kosorica square. Would the wounding of two civilians be an unusual incident and would it be mentioned in this report?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had such information, it would certainly have been included in the report because civilians were victims. If we had any such information, we would inform the Main Staff so that measures could be taken and for them to be able to help us do that. But at the time, as I said, we had no such information and consequently couldn't inform them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And item 8 says you expect frequent injuries and losses on our side, and you say that it is very difficult for our soldiers and officers to remain patient and restrain themselves from responding with effective fire. Does the Main Staff approve of such more vigorous return of fire or do you stand by your restraint?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the activities of the corps are concerned, unless explicit orders are received then the tasks are carried out in line with earlier orders. And these are in line with the principles of warfare in the city. Whether and how there will be responses, whether there will be extensive reactions or proportionate, that's left to the commanders who decide about the kind of fire and the weapons they will use at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did not return with effective fire and what is effective fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is effective fire depends on the target. When an order was issued to neutralise a target, then the fire was effective, then the -- when the target was neutralised or if the order was destroy the target, then it is effective if the target was indeed destroyed; if it wasn't, it was not effective. The quantity of ammunition for the destruction of a target can be six times higher than the quantity needed to neutralise a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't need to call up a document. It was admitted with General Galic, D24 -- 3429.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says enemy provocations are continuing, the consequence of which is the exhaustion of soldiers because they respond only exceptionally so that the question as to how long they would be able to restrain themselves is moving into the foreground. I read this from item 8, forecasts and conclusions. You saw the document. The document of the 4th doesn't mention the incident on Ivana Krndelj Street either. Why?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that we had no information about that incident nor did anyone inform us nor did anyone protest. All our information was received much later after the war speaking about this specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you say in the report of the 4th that you refrained from returning fire, does that mean that you did so on the following day as well?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says we continued to exercise restraint, then it applies to the following day as well unless there is a report to show the opposite. I've already said what that restraint means and for what reasons it can be given up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. The answer's already been given, but just another caution to Dr. Karadzic in the phrasing of his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Line 23 should read the previous day rather than the following day. Because I was asking about the previous day, the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That applies to the 3rd of September as well. Yes, I confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D06305, please. It's dated the 5th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the 5th of September and it is again stated that the enemy violated the truce agreement. And paragraph 4 says sniper fire throughout the day on Grbavica and Lukavica from the point of town where the Muslims are and from Mojmilo. And item 7, could we scroll down to find it.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please scroll down the Serbian version too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, not the second page. In the Serbian version it is at the bottom and we need item 7 in English too. You say here under "losses," that two soldiers were seriously wounded by enemy snipers in the zone of responsibility of the Vogosca TG and the names are Dobro Kojic and Boro Gavric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the following page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the conclusions you say that the enemy is still violating the cease-fire and intensifying sniper fire. You expect them to continue with provocations in the coming period. In this report for the 5th of September, there is nothing about Ivana Krndelj Street, but it is said that the Muslim side is intensifying its sniper fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing about the events in Dobrinja and in Ivana Krndelj Street and it's surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D01618, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it to appear on the screen, General, did the international factor paid you attention to the Serbian casualties in Grbavica and Ilidza, did they voice a protest about that as they voiced protests when something happened to the other side?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that everyone is more sensitive about his or her own casualties. If the casualties are greater in number, then the sensitivity of either side is greater. So to assess whether a third party understood us or them and understood the incidents properly, it can be said that the attitude internationally, in the international media and the international politics, was such that they leaned to the BH Army and its 1st Corps. And therefore, all the commands and institutions of the mass media were sent to the BH Army territory in Sarajevo, whereas on the side of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps we had military observers and one part of the units depending on the stage of the war that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the attitude to our casualties in the media and in UN reports, what was it like?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult from this point in time to provide an overall assessment, but from how I understood it then it's different when you assess it from this point in time than if you assessed it then. I then believed that our losses were not considered sufficiently and that the casualties on the Serbian side, not just Serbs but in our territory, were not valued as much as casualties and incidents that occurred in the territory under the control of the 1st Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us look at your report dated the 24th of October, 1993, 1700 hours, where in paragraph 4 you say that Browning fired and sniper fire on Dobrinja, Grbavica, and Lukavica and that one woman was killed by sniper fire in Grbavica today. We see that Nafa Taric was wounded and that is included in the indictment as an incident, and in Grbavica a woman was killed, and God knows which incident this was in which Serb civilians lost their lives, and once again you did not respond. There's only observation and reconnaissance as we can see under item 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, if Dr. Karadzic is going to persist in reading out the document when we can all see it, maybe he should get it right because at page 53, line 20, he said: We see that Nafa Taric was wounded. The document doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have dealt with the incident dated the 3rd of September in which Nafa Taric and her daughter were wounded, and in this instance a woman was killed. And that was the basis for my question what sort of attention was paid to Serbian casualties. It's not in this document, that's true, but it is mentioned in the previous document, or rather, in the indictment. Here let me avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell me how many civilian casualties were needed for you to decide to respond?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question. It depended on many factors whether we would decide, take the decision, to violate the truce if it was in force. We have said what the circumstances were under which one could violate the truce and order fire only if there was great necessity. So I would not repeat. I have already said that once. But what is important here in my view is what was going on in Grbavica. We said previously that there were many civilian losses there and what was the ratio -- well, every now and then there would be some civilian casualty in Grbavica which confirms what I observed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 21 I would rather say "ultimate necessity" than "great necessity."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So "ultimate necessity" or "great necessity," what did you say?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimate necessity, ultimate necessity, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The indictment also includes an incident dated the 2nd of November, 1993, in which Ramiza Kundo according to the indictment was wounded while she was carrying a pail of water and crossing Brijesko Brdo Street which is now called Bulbulistan. Did you order fire to be opened then and there or was it somebody else who ordered it and then reported to you that such an incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the area above the railway station in Rajlovac as far as I can remember, and there were some railway cars parked there. I did not receive any report about it then. We discussed that incident just like all other sniping incidents, so I did receive several pieces of information about it. But this area, if we look at our map again, which was a colour map, it's better than the one which is enclosed, I mean the one from the 1st Corps of the BH Army. And if we then see the deployment of the brigade in Brijesce Brdo we will see that they did have forces deployed in that area. Now, what was there, what forces were there? At the time when the incident occurred, there is nothing specific that I can say about that apart from the general disposition of forces. One piece of information during the discussion about the incident was that the position was not sufficiently visible from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber who was at a dominant position and who was at a lower position, which forces? Who is at Brijesce Brdo and who or where were the Serbian forces with regard to Brijesce Brdo or in relation to Brijesce Brdo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the date was October --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were in the area of Azici and down towards the Dobrinja river, and on Brijesce Brdo there was the 2nd Mountain Brigade I -- no, motorised brigade or whatever. So the 1st Corps of the BH Army was at Brijesce Brdo and its forces were in the area. It was one brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Galic. Did you refer to a date when answering the question? If so, please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I repeated the date. That was during the month of October 1993. Just to have some bearing in time because this was a continuing process. This is why I mentioned the date from this daily report, October, but let us say the day as well, the 24th of October, 1993, so if we were to say where our forces were, they were in Azici holding that area and Brijesce Brdo and the surrounding area where the incident occurred was in the zone of the BH Army 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 2nd of November -- oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please speak a bit more slowly. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You told us about Brijesce Brdo. Just tell us briefly who was on top of the slope and who was in the valley and where did the incident occur, was it up or down?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to explain but I was interrupted. That is why I will now repeat. Brijesce Brdo and that area of Sokol which continues on to Zuc, an elevation which dominates in this area, and above the area of Azici in the direction of Rajlovac and Ilidza as well. So our forces were at the foot of this hill. And the incident happened on the hill. It's a part of the hill or the foot of the hill, how should I put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D1622.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document dates from the previous day, General. We can see what the enemy was doing, and under item 2 the document says that our forces responded and returned fire in the sectors where the enemy grouped and the points from which there was strong fire. This order dated the 1st of November to return only fire at the sectors where they are grouping their forces and the points from which there was fire, was it changed on another day, on the next day, the 2nd of November? So was it still in force, this order, was it in force for the following day?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell anymore whether it was valid for the following day because so many years have passed. I really cannot remember. I really cannot answer this question. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, was it usual to change the manner of conduct and the way activities were carried out without any orders?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For any change of order, approval had to be sought, unless it was already covered by what was ordered previously and unless the possibility was allowed for someone to independently decide to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if this Ramiza Kundo on Brijesce Brdo were really wounded by the Serbian forces, is that something that would be in accordance with the permission or order of the corps or was there any military target on Brijesce Brdo that could have been targeted possibly?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Brijesce Brdo one battalion of that brigade was deployed. That was more or less the strength, and its disposition was in this zone. Now, where this civilian was at that particular moment, certainly in the disposition zone or deployment zone of the 1st Corps. Now, whether there were any troops in the immediate vicinity, that's something that I couldn't tell you from this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is another incident dated the 6th of January, 1994, in which a lady - let me not mention her name - was shot, that's incident 6, the last part. She was shot in her bottom while she was crossing the bridge in Nikola Demonja Street in Dobrinja on a bicycle. The same question: Did you order, did anyone -- any one of your subordinates order such fire? And did you receive a report about this wounding? The bicycle was moving across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Dobrinja. The person was wounded just above the seat of the bicycle.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer is the same as with previous. We have seen incidents with sniping or shelling, whatever you call them. I did not receive any report nor did I issue orders to fire on that area because if there was fire then it was infantry fire. The corps commander rarely or only under exceptional circumstances orders that specific fire be opened in specific areas. Now whether some of the subordinate units did it, I did not receive a report that someone ordered such fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at ... [In English] I see Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just a piece of information. Page 59, lines 13 and 14, I don't think that General Galic exactly said that. For the second sentence: "We have seen incidents with shelling or sniping, whatever you call them." I just wanted to draw your attention on this in case of future problems with that part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to slow down when answering questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue but please bear in mind speaking very slowly, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I'm sure that I remember what you said but we can always listen to the tape. You said about that incident as well as about other previous incidents, you didn't say we saw incidents involving sniping and shelling, you didn't say that you saw any such thing?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to repeat what I said for the clarity's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When we're talking about this particular incident, the same applies as to any other sniping incidents in the indictment or indictments. I never received any reports about any of those incidents. I never received information that anybody had ordered fire to be opened in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the report issued one day before, on the 1st --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, we have never received this document. I would like to call up 65 ter 2393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, just before we get to another document, I'd just like to put on the record that D3451 was actually a daily combat report and not an order, as Dr. Karadzic said at the last line of page 57, the beginning of page 58, that's D3451 is a daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's clarify that as well. This is not the document that I called up. I asked for 65 ter 23903.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, if you or your command reported on the conduct on the 1st of November, did it comport itself in keeping with the orders?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see here, the command acted in accordance with the previous orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this particular day when that alleged incident involving the lady on the bicycle took place at the end of that day, it's at 1800 hours, it was already dark and everything had calmed down apparently. Let's see if we can find that incident anywhere here. I don't see it. It says that the enemy carried out several successive infantry attacks against our positions in Grbavica and Ilidza and that over 120 shells fell on Ilidza. They were 120-millimetre shells. And then under 2 it says that the Serb forces were involved in defence activities. And whenever targets were discovered fire was opened. There were no major successes due to very strong defence. And now under 5 it says that there is a desire among a number of soldiers to spend their -- spend Christmas Eve and Christmas with their families. So security of our positions may be threatened in that case. We saw earlier today one of the sniping incidents happened on Serbian Easter. For the participants, I would like to say that the 6th of January is Christmas Eve and the 7th of January is Christmas according to the Julian calendar --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic isn't here giving a speech nor is he having a conversation with the General, and so perhaps he could be encouraged to start this question again and actually ask the question rather than repeat the contents of the document for whatever purpose I don't understand actually.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall establish a link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But while the Prosecution will not challenge that the specific date was Christmas Eve or Christmas Day on Orthodox religion, but do not -- refrain from making comments. It is a rather lengthy comment. Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could have asked the witness but that would have taken up some time. I could have asked him about those holidays and those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember from one of the previous documents that one sniping incident took place on the Serbian Easter and now we are talking about the Serbian Christmas Eve. There was sniping activities on that day. Let me ask you, did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps have more activities during Muslim holidays or did it refrain itself from activities on those days?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Sarajevo, people knew each other although they waged a war against each other. They didn't know me. I was not a resident of Sarajevo, but they knew each other. They called to -- up to each other. I was in Rajlovac when I heard them calling each other. So they knew and they were familiar with the customs of the area. They could even joke with each other during the war and of course they respected each other's holidays, and then a thing like that happened. But that was not a rule. However, incidents did happen on both sides. We wanted to celebrate holidays peacefully, not only Sarajevo but everywhere else. We wanted peaceful Muslims as well as for ourselves. I remember a request by the commander of the Egyptian Battalion. He addressed me in writing, although I had invited him to come to my office. He was headquartered in the Marsal Tito barracks in the territory of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. He asked us not to display any activities during that time. I wanted to talk to him and tell him that as much as possible I would prevent any such activities during the Ramadan and similar religious holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document nothing is reported about fire that was opened on the bridge where the lady was wounded?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's remind ourselves that that was the bridge across the Dobrinja and I don't see a reference to any activities across that bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the indictment there is another incident which allegedly happened on the 25th of May, 1994. One 53-year-old woman and another 62-year-old woman were wounded in the legs while riding on a bus full of passengers at the crossroads of Nikola Demonja Street and the JNA boulevard. Currently, it is the crossroads of the Nikola Demonja Street and the defenders of Dobrinja avenue in Dobrinja. Two women -- two passengers on the bus were wounded in the legs. In other words, on the 25th of May, 1994, was an order issued? Was it approved to open fire on a civilian bus or a bus full of civilians?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this distance when I look back and when I remember that buses were running, that people could stroll, that they could work in their gardens, that they could go shopping, I asked myself: What else could we do? What else could we make possible in that area? If public transport was working in the area of Dobrinja which was under constant fire as it were and if people were wounded, the question is: Who wounded them and whether we could open fire on that bus from our side. A bus in that area -- I remember some of the footages that were shown from a subsequent period of time, where one could see that some people were not that serious when they opened fire on either buses or trams. There was a ban on opening fire on public transport means because it was well-known that passengers were mostly civilians; however, if it was discovered that troops were being transported, then that would have been a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you learn that some of your subordinates had approved fire opening on the bus on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't receive reports to that effect. I don't remember that I ever received a report on a bus having been a target in Dobrinja. If you have a document that speaks to the contrary, I would like to see it; but as far as I can remember, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, just a while ago you addressed a topic that I would like to follow-up on. During the 1200 or 1300 days of war in Sarajevo, what is your view of the fact that the indictment includes the wounding of people that happened in such large intervals? What can you tell us about the freedom of movement, the activities of the civilians and civilian transport means? And can you put all that in the perspective of possible incidents that happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I don't think I follow the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nor do I at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show another document. I wanted to show you what I received by way of a report on that date. It will take me only a couple of minutes and while the topic is still fresh on our minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue but I couldn't understand your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I'll come back to that report later. I would like to call up 65 ter 7042. 7042, 65 ter, yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a report which was sent to me, to the president of Republika Srpska, by the Main Staff. Look at the zone of responsibility of the SRK in the fourth paragraph where I was informed about the activities of the enemy, sniping fire on Vrbanja bridge, Zlatiste, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page. Can we go to the following page in English? Bullet point 2(c).

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was informed that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps observed the cease-fire. It was engaged in reconnaissance of the enemy activity. The point is that had you been informed about that incident, would you have reported back to the Main Staff and would the Main Staff have reported back to me?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had received a report about that incident that had happened, I'm sure that I would have conveyed that to the Main Staff. I don't know and can't say for a fact that the Main Staff would have conveyed that message to you as well, but I am almost sure that it would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With regard to you and your knowledge from the field, what would you say about the president's knowledge about the situation on the ground? What did the president know and where did he receive his information from?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What president? I knew a lot of presidents. I knew a lot of presidents of the Main Boards or municipalities. Which president?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He may be in a position to be aware of the sources of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I have known more than the information that I received from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer that question, but I wanted you to be precise in terms of what president you had in mind because some other presidents also received reports along their own chains of information. The Ministry of the Interior sent its reports and I suppose that reports were also sent by the intelligence services and all the other segments that were at the very top of and close to the command of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and you were its supreme commander of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 18 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To be clearer and put things simpler with regard to the question that I seem to have phrased in a too complicated fashion, during the war in Sarajevo which lasted 1200 or 1300 days but you were only there during 1.000 days or so, did civilians walk about freely, go to shops, have cultural events, go to mosques or churches, and have public transportation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depended on the development of the situation in the respective part of town or the period of time. There were times when there were soccer matches between UNPROFOR and the BH Army, but on the whole –- well, of the measures we took we made an effort to spare civilians and not let them become war victims. No matter how far the law reaches in the humanitarian sense, war did progress in a negative way. With the development of various techniques, tactics and operations, civilian losses grew even greater. Let me mention what I read, that during the First World War civilian losses accounted for 5 per cent; in the Second World War, 45 per cent; Korean War, 85 per cent; Vietnam War, 90 per cent, and it's as high as 96 per cent in Iraq. I don't know how accurate this data is, but they do tell us something. The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to some sources, had 56 per cent of civilian losses. The latest estimates say that the overall losses were 100.000, and that's the estimate of that institute in Sarajevo, and 40 per cent of that number are civilian victims. And the share of civilian losses in Sarajevo was 36 per cent, according to the data while I was in command, according to OTP data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the indictment against me there is a sniping incident and allegedly happened on the 19th of June, 1994, when on a tram which was moving from Carsija westward, Jasmina Kucinar and her son, aged 4, were slightly wounded in the legs. Mensur Jusic, likewise, Belma Sukic, and so on. The tram was near the Holiday Inn at that time. Did you issue an order on or around the 19th of June to launch such activities or did you have information about any subordinates to have ordered anything like it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remembered that at that time there was discussion about restarting tram traffic in Sarajevo, and that was done in contacts between the UNPROFOR representatives for BH and the Main Staff. It was decided that trams should start again, and public transportation in general, and we received an order to that effect. All speculation about the impossibility to have public transportation on both sides depended on the current situation at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Based on orders of higher commands, could you and did you give permission and orders to shoot at public transportation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I see we're going into another topic quite squarely and I apologise for not rising sooner, but at the beginning of this session Dr. Karadzic put a question to the witness claiming on his part that the war in Sarajevo lasted 1200 or 1300 days and telling the witness he was only there for 1.000 of that, which is not evidence, only comment, inappropriate and, I would submit, misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's an approximation. It may not have been 1.000 days exactly, but on the whole the war in Sarajevo lasted over 1200 days. From the 6th of April till the peace, that's more 1200 days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was commander for 23 months, so that may be around that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue. Probably it's better for you, Mr. Karadzic, to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have approval from the higher command to order or tolerate shooting at buses, trams, and other public transportation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All civilian facilities or persons or protected facilities could not be fired at. Nobody had the right to issue such an order. The conclusion that somebody ordered fire on buses and trams is false. If there was such instances, then I should have been informed or the brigade command because there were military observers there, and then I'm certain that measures could be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You already said that the UNPROFOR never informed you about individual sniping incidents but only -- you only got general information. Were you ever invited to delegate somebody to the commission to investigate such incidents?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been waiting for this question because little has been said about it. The truth is like this: We were for the establishment of Joint Commissions at the level of the Main Staff and the UNPROFOR staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was a commission called the lower joint military commission formed at the corps level. The commission included a representative of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, one of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, and one of the UNPROFOR Sarajevo sector. And they were supposed to investigate all these incidents, but following orders of the Joint Commission at the level of General Staffs. So they didn't have the right to do anything without an order and without their safety being guaranteed. I only remember that we sent a representative of our corps, I'm speaking about Lieutenant-Colonel Ugresic, to take part in the work of that commission, and it happened at the airport, to report to General Razek, and the -- it was as usual: The Serbs are to blame. This was about an attack on the forces and equipment of UNPROFOR at Butmir airport, but the commission established that the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army were responsible for that. It is interesting that the commission never met after that incident, although we requested that whenever there's a problem of any kind the commissions should meet and find out what it's all about. That's how it wanted to investigate the Markale incident too and General Gvero insisted on that. The situation at the airport and the investigation of that incident are something that Lieutenant-Colonel Ugresic also testified about. He died unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1754, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see a report dated 18 June 1994. That's one day before the 19th of June and incident number 8 on the F list. Here it is. Please take a look. Item 2 reads: "Our forces. "Units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps honour the cease-fire. At the lines reached the units are engaged in additional monitoring." Let us take a look at item 8. Here we have item 8: Conclusions, forecasts, and decision. "It is expected that the enemy will continue to carry out provocations and combat activities with which he wishes to provoke our forces to reply to provocations and jeopardise the signed truce." And the following sentence: "Continue to fully and consistently implement the agreement on the cessation of combat activities." Is this an order, sir?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can be interpreted as an order, but judging by the heading I would say it's a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this item, conclusions, forecast, and decision?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision is stated for the superior command to see whether the decision is all right or not. How could the Main Staff react to the corps command's decisions? Because it cannot have their people present in every corps command. We mostly had the representatives around when something important was happening or when we're launching significant military operations along certain axes. Here the conclusion, or rather, this demand is very interesting. I don't know if you want me to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you can be brief, go ahead, especially from the point of view of the incident that happened on the following day.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the Bobovac Brigade here which had its positions in the direction of Varos, and we must create conditions to cut the line towards that area where that HVO Brigade was located, but I cannot link this to the incident in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in connection with Sarajevo, this report dated the 18th of June, does it allow for the possibility of somebody shooting from infantry weapons or snipers at a tram?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on these conclusions and forecasts and the decision itself, which is partly reproduced here, no shooting at the city can be expected, especially not at public transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3454, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us take a short look at D2668, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a report dated 19 June. Oh, that's probably the one -- yes, this is it. Now page 2 in Serbian. Conclusions, expectations, and decision. It says: "Continue to implement the agreement on the cessation of combat activities. Expect that the enemy will continue with provocations in order to endanger the agreed cease-fire." General, had there be firing at public transportation would that have been mentioned in this report? Is the Main Staff informed of all combat activities?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was sent by the subordinate units to the corps command or what the corps command found out personally in the zone under the command of the corps or if we received any information from other sources, we then wanted to and did present it to the Main Staff command. So if we had information that public transportation vehicles were fired at, if someone fired and did fire, we would certainly report this to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is another incident under number 9 on the F list in the indictment. The date is the 26th of June, 1994. Supposedly Sanela Muratovic was wounded in her right shoulder while walking along Djure Jaksic Street with a female friend of hers. Now it's Adija Mulabegovic Street in the western part of Sarajevo. General, did you or anyone from the corps order or allow fire at that street, or rather, at a 16-year-old girl in that street on the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find my bearings and remember where the street is. I told you earlier that I did not live in Sarajevo so it's very difficult for me to find my bearings around the various neighbourhoods and streets. When you mention them it's a great problem for me, but not such a great problem that I could not answer your question. I can tell you that certainly, like with anything else that had to do with the protection of the civilians and the order which I issued, if we have that in mind no one ordered or should have ordered any sort of disturbing the civilians or attack against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at D2554 for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report sent to the Main Staff at 1700 hours, a regular combat report for the 26th of June, 1994. Could we please see page 2. We need item 8. Could you please read item 8, the first two paragraphs. I'm not sure what was translated. This is an admitted document; however, item 8 --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- conclusions --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- conclusions, expectations, and decisions about further activities. Considering the enemy activities --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering the enemy activities, it is still to be expected that there would be significant fire in provocation at our defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the next two lines as well, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continue to implement the agreement on the truce consistently and refrain from combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What sort of conclusion would you then draw on the basis of the order and decision on further activities in view of the incident which supposedly occurred on the 26th of June, 1994? Could that have happened with the knowledge or with the approval not to say at the -- on the order of the commands?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see that restraint from further combat activities is ordered here, that means both active combat operations and manoeuvres of the forces and also any firing, that they should refrain from that. So no incident should happen and it was not allowed to happen in that period. If such an incident did occur and if we had been aware of it, we would have had to mention it in this report, process it in some sort way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D01 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm wondering why we do not have a matching English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was asking Mr. Reid the same question. The English translation that's here was done by, our records read, the Defence in General Galic's trial. This was an associated exhibit with Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for some reason the fact that the English translation was incomplete wasn't noticed and not raised in court and the Prosecution made no objection to it. Regardless, the English translation is still incomplete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I'm not sure whether this English translation is part of the original document. Can we see the first page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The reference number reads the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It appears to be a translation of paragraph 1 alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So shall we mark it for identification pending the English translation is complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's been admitted as an exhibit already, but if you want to reclassify it in any event we'll go ahead and request a complete translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, in order not to forget. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will reclassify it as marked for identification pending English translation. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have 1D01760.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Two days before the last incident your regular combat report, or rather, the report from your command, Cedo Sladoje was probably the person who signed it, please look at the third paragraph which reads: "Today at 1415 hours, Koviljka Krajisnik from Zabrdje was killed by a sniper bullet to the heart. The bullet came from the direction of Sokolj." And with all due piety, do you know what was the relation of the woman who was killed with our parliament speaker, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see here, first of all, that the one month cessation of hostilities was still in force in the beginning under enemy, so any firing or activities in the Sarajevo zone was prohibited. As for the incident, Zabrdje is a village between Rajlovac and Vogosca in the direction of Zuc. And this family used to live there. I'm saying they used to live there because as far as I know they no longer live there today. She is probably related in one way or another to our parliament speaker I suppose, but I cannot say that with certainty. Judging by the surname she should be. And very often we are related by the common surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I be allowed to say that she was his daughter-in-law. Under item 2, let us see what our forces are doing. They are observing the agreement on the truce. The commanders of certain units are making a tour of certain positions and lines in order to review the troops and to remove any shortcomings. And then there's a warning that unnecessary firing should stop. There are courses for units which are about to begin and so on and so forth. How often did commanding officers visit or tour the first front line? Was that done with your knowledge or at your orders?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers from the corps command toured the front line in accordance with a plan and also on my order, which is normal. I personally also made tours of units and commands in the entire zone of the defence of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. All those activities were organised in a planned manner as much as that was possible, but there were always many extraordinary circumstances and unusual incidents so that these plans had to be changed very often. Because if we plan for today to visit, for example, the Vogosca Brigade, and then there are problems on the Nisici plateau, or if we have a breakthrough, an enemy breakthrough in that area, then it's certain that that part of the command would go to the area where the positions of our side are jeopardised or if there are major losses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see item 8 on the following page in both languages. In the English language it's possibly the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, here also the last sentence under item 8 says: "Consistently implement the agreement on the cessation of hostilities and put up decisive resistance to defend the lines reached." Two days before the incident, was it then prohibited to open fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we follow the order and it says that it's a one-month cessation of hostilities rather than a cease-fire. I think it was called cessation of hostilities. So it was normal that we had to stick to the order and carry out the tasks as set out in the order. So that would be everything that I could say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3455, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Incident number 10 on the F list in my indictment has to do with an incident that occurred on the 22nd of July, 1994, and according to the indictment, supposedly Sead Solak, a 13-year-old who was shot and wounded in his belly while together with his mother and sister. He was window-shopping in Miljenka Cvitkovica Street, currently Ferde Hauptmana Street in Cengic villa section of Sarajevo. What was your knowledge of the situation as regards the orders issued on that day with regard to firing at civilians, and did you receive any report about such an incident?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the incidents, individual incidents, about which we have stated our conclusions previously. I did not receive any reports about this incident during the war nor was I aware of it. I learned about it during my trial later on. The area in question is Cengic villa and we can see if we look at the disposition which forces were deployed there, but there is some information available that there was some unit or troops that were deployed or were moving in that particular area. Now, whether there was any firing, what sort of fire or activities, that is something that I could not claim at this point in time and in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose troops would be moving around Cengic villa at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cengic villa, that's the Sarajevo down-town, the very centre of the city, so that was -- that would have been the troops of the 1st Corps of the BH Army or the troops belonging to the Supreme Command because they had their special units, the MUP was there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2994 is the document we would need to look at now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade was deployed?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd, in this period the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade -- it was set up a bit later than the Rajlovac Brigade, the Vogosca Brigade, and the Kosevo or Centar Brigade, depending on how we called it at which point. The 3rd Sarajevo Brigade was in charge of that area, Rajlovac, Vogosca, and a part stretching in the direction of Hresa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it in the zone of Cengic villa?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Sarajevo? The 3rd Sarajevo was in the opposite part of town. There was no chance to -- for activities by the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade in the area of Cengic villa. I can't see from which positions they could have fired at Cengic villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please focus on item 2 now so that we wouldn't deal with everything else. Item 2 says: "Our forces did not respond to occasional enemy fire except for the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, the units of which responded with fire from infantry" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bear in mind that we do not seem to have English translation other than the paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please read out item 2 and the first paragraph of item 2?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. Item 2: "Our forces did not respond to occasional enemy fire, except for the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade whose units returned fire from infantry weapons at observed enemy points."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this be linked with Cengic villa, this firing by the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the disposition of such forces was such that they could not have done anything in the direction of Cengic villa. It was possible to fire with mortars - but I don't know what else - in the direction of Cengic villa. But with a rifle or any other infantry weapon it was not possible, because the distance was too great nor was there any suitable location from which to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And down under item 3, situation in the territory, it says: "Due to sniper fire at Trebevicka and Ohridska Street, the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, UNPROFOR has been informed, then their representatives came out to the spot immediately and conducted an on-site investigation. Where are the Trebevicka and Ohridska streets located? Who had that under their control?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebevicka and Ohridska Street, as far as I can remember, are close to the Jewish cemetery. I may be mistaken in which case I apologise because you know the situation better than I do. I believe that Trebevicka Street is there and it continues or rather it extends into the Jewish cemetery and onwards to Debelo Brdo. In other words, that part of Trebevicka Street -- I believe I've answered your question, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit MFI D3456.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to add something. Maybe I have not said everything or maybe my words have not been recorded properly. That area was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. That's what I wanted to add to my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at another document dated 27 July 1994, 1D01788. General, sir, could you please help us. Look at the first paragraph where it says that during the preceding 24 hours the enemy did not respect the cease-fire and the document goes on to say that it attacked Beogradska Street with rifle grenades and that sniper fire was opened on Sedrenik. Who controlled Sedrenik at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sedrenik, as far as I can understand, this may be confusing, but Sedrenik was under the control of the 1st Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, your men reported to you that they had opened fire on Sedrenik; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I can read here and I can only confirm that Sedrenik was within the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BiH army; it was not under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page bullet point 10. I'm looking for the same in English. It says that in Sucuri Dobrinja settlement, one woman was wounded. Who controlled that settlement, Sucuri?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sucuri settlement is close to Mojmilo, but Sucuri was within the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. We controlled that area. Dobrinja is also in that area and the so-called Sucura houses are in that area, a bit below Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to the report, was that woman a civilian? If she was not a civilian, would that be clear from the report?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It always says in the report when a soldier was wounded. If it says just a woman, it is self-explanatory. At one point, though, we had a battalion of women in Ilidza but it was disbanded; however, whenever it says a woman, that implies that the person was also a civilian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3457, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I would like to move on to a different topic. I would like to discuss the issue of UNPROFOR and military observers of the United Nations and relationship between the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and those structures. What was your position with regard to the co-operation and relationship with UNPROFOR and UNMOs, UNMO standing for the military observers of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already shared with you my general position, or rather, the way I understood their role and what my attitude was towards UNPROFOR and UNMOs. I considered them an integral part of the implementation of all those things that were part of the customs of war of everything that was envisaged by the 1949 Geneva Conventions and their Protocols. So if they didn't do their job properly, we were not in a position to comply with our obligations. If we did not co-operate with them, we also could not comply with our obligations. In the territory of the 1st Corps of the BiH army in Sarajevo, the front line didn't move much. How could I be informed what was going on there? We had our reconnaissance missions. We relied on people who crossed over, and one of our major sources whom I trusted were them. I trusted them. When the information was wrong, I did not think that it was intentional, that it was intended to deceive the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Whatever information they received, they conveyed it to me and this is visible from the report that we saw the other day. That relationship was also based on the fact that we issued orders to our subordinated units, telling them how to treat those forces and their representatives. Whoever represented them and whoever visited us, even not on an official visit, they could all address me directly or any other body in the command. In our corps command which operated next to the ten UNMOs whose office was next to mine, I had a battalion of the legion of foreigners from France sitting next to me, and I had 90-millimetre self-propelled guns in front of the corps command, three of them that belonged to the French Battalion. I am speeding, I apologise. I'll wait a little. I wanted to build our relationship on mutual trust and understanding, on mutual respect as well. I respected all the commanders whose mission in Sarajevo was not easy. They did not have an easy task, but my task was also not easy. Nobody had an easy time in Sarajevo at that time. That's why I sympathised with them more than they could ever understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you just said that you believed that if they misinformed you they didn't do it on purpose, but they just conveyed the information that they had received. Who did they receive their information from? Who may have provided them with misinformation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's remind ourselves, we had a map before us giving an overview of UNMOs on the side of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. They covered 11 different points. And we also saw that on the side of the 1st Corps of the BiH army there were eight - that's what I said - but I only saw four positions. I didn't count them. So I accept that the schematic that we saw was more accurate than my information because I didn't really know how many of them there were on the Muslim side. They received information and reports from the military observers who were deployed in the territory of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. They also received reports from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was in Sarajevo. They were in constant communication with them and they did not communicate constantly with you in Pale. Whatever problem had to be shared, whatever information had to be shared, they would go to see Ganic or Alija or the corps commander or the chief of the Main Staff, and they would receive information about whatever issue was at stake and they received that information. Since that information came from important high places and from important people, I suppose that they did not double-check that information but rather sent that information directly to us, and sometimes that information was not exactly accurate that -- and that we already saw in the reports that were before us already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they always properly marked? What kind of orders and instructions did you give to your subordinate commands with regard to the international forces, the United Nations forces, in Sarajevo? When I say "properly marked," I mean their vehicles, their staffs, their observation posts. Were they properly and well marked? What kind of instructions did you give to your subordinate units with regard to their safety?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever they were deployed in our zone of responsibility, in the zone of responsibility of the Romanija -- Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, my order was to provide them with the best possible conditions of life and work. My instructions were to fully co-operate with those people, with the representatives of the military observers. Likewise, they were marked. Their vehicles were marked by UN markings. Their uniforms were UN uniforms. And you could also tell which national army they were affiliated to. For example, the French Foreign Legion soldiers wore their own uniforms but they also bore UN markings by which they could be distinguished from some other troops, for example, Egyptian, Russian or others that joined them subsequently in Grbavica. That part of our position or attitude towards them, I believe that should have been or should have led to more help from them. When we were withdrawing from Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica in the territory of Tresnja Brdo towards Golo Brdo and when they were supposed to take over positions from us, they were attacked by the 1st Corps of the BiH Army, so we had to protect them and we had to fight with them against the forces of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army. They gave us a certain degree of recognition, but you can't find it in any of their reports. Nowhere will you find an account of that help that we gave them in performing their mission. Our units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps helped them whenever and wherever they could. For example, various convoys passed through our territory in winter-time and in summertime. The roads were not conducive to their passage. Very often they would skid from the road and we helped them. Some of those things will be seen in the documents that you are going to show. There are a lot of those things. I want to be economical with time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
