utterances.text: Mr. Galic, let me go back to the issue of misinformation. I note that word is used by Mr. Karadzic, not by you, but you said -- what you said is this. It's page 85, line 2: "When the information was wrong, I did not think that it was intentional, that it was intended to deceive the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps." While you -- let me confine it to the sniping incidents. While you did not know whether it happened or not, how do you know that information -- certain information was wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about the information that was presented to the corps command by UNPROFOR. I'm sure you will remember a document that we analysed here in this courtroom. In that document they say - if I'm not mistaken - that fire had been opened at Colina Kapa and we replied that in that area there were no Muslim forces at that time and that there was no need to open fire on that area. Now, who provided them with that information? I don't know. It's not up to me. But that information at that moment was inaccurate or any other such inaccurate information for that matter. I would answer them along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to the sniping issues again, and Mr. Karadzic presented you - I think it's ten, ten incidents referred to in the indictment, schedule F (1) to schedule F(10) - and Mr. Karadzic repeatedly asked you every time with respect to those sniping incidents whether you or somebody else ordered such firing and whether you received any report about those incidents. And your answers were all no to every question. But at certain point of time, it's page 58, line 10 to 12, you alluded to the possibility of independent firing by someone and also you said this, it's at page 15 from lines 15 to 19, when you were answering a question to a specific protest. This is what you said: "For example, what I know today, what you know today, what the Courts know today, I didn't know that at that time, that somebody got killed from sniping fire. How was I supposed to know that? I did not receive such information and I could not react because there was no information of that kind." Do you remember having said that, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no dilemma whether I said it or not. This is what I did say. But the context is important. The question is important, to which I answered that -- I'm sure that I did say that, but give me the context or give me the question to what I answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of that context this is a question for you, Mr. Galic. From what you know today in light of what you know or you have heard today, do you exclude the possibilities that the victims referred to in the indictment were killed by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on what I know today and we also investigated after that, I mean during my trial and after the trial, I can say that the victims mentioned here, I cannot deny. I can't say that these incidents didn't happen. The evidence available now shows that some incidents happened, no doubt. But at the time, I repeat, I did not have such evidence because things were not put to me with the same arguments from UNPROFOR, the enemy forces, and the various commissions who went to the site to check whether it was possible that fire came from here or from there, if I had had all that information I would have viewed things differently. I can say something else to show my honesty, besides I'm under oath so I must speak the truth and nothing but the truth. If the prosecutor started the trial against me with 37 sniping incidents, and if they had given up ten, or rather, they gave up ten and confined himself to 23, that is, 40 per cent were given up immediately, now based on new evidence we are contesting 12 of these incidents out of 23. But one of the Judges also accepted the evidence that we led during the trial but the other members of the Chamber did not accept it. Now I would have to give it another thought whether an individual incident happened or not. This would be my reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave it at that. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, His Excellency, Judge Kwon, asked you if it was possible that this was committed by Serbian forces. What would -- how would you interpret "Serbian forces" in this context with regard to your command and your ability of acting as a commander?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpret it in this context as meaning the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. But if we remind ourselves of what we mentioned before and namely the existence of various paramilitaries and the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BH Army who even were in combat with their own forces, then it could be also interpreted in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is any Serb with a rifle in the zone of responsibility of the SRK part of Serbian forces for which you are responsible?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that person is under my command, then I'm responsible. But in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps after my arrival I had quite some problems with some paramilitaries that were not under the command of the corps. Let me immediately clarify what we call paramilitaries. It's not the same thing as the English term. A paramilitary, to our understanding, is anybody who is not under the command of the commander of that territory, be it an individual or a unit. And I always used to say that a paramilitary can only be created by para authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the topic of co-operation or relations with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, General, let me ask you if it was difficult to procure weapons with optical sights just before the war or in the early days of the war?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, or rather, in the early stage of the war -- well, it may have been less difficult for some people to procure some weapons than for others. But the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army were better-placed to procure such weapons because of the factory that was located on their side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document number is 1D01147. If we can have that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me follow-up on my previous reply. The forces of the BH Army were in a position to come by more modern sniping rifles importing them from abroad, whereas we didn't have so much opportunity to do so. And while they were co-operating with the HVO, they had -- it was even easier for them to come by such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at your report to the Main Staff dated the 14th of September, 1992. I'm interested in item 6 on page 2 of the original, whereas in English it's on the first page. It says here that you as a corps commander met with the commander of the UN observer forces sector. You spoke about flights, humanitarian aid, demilitarisation, and then you say: "Mutual understanding and trust in resolving these issues was expressed." You spoke about it a short while ago. Was this what you meant, this sentence in this report?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the date again? I don't remember it. It's 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 14 September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must inquire about the date to know who this commander of the Sarajevo sector was at the time, and it was General Razek. We wanted to have extensive co-operation with him and we would do what we could to assist him. The issue of the Sarajevo airport included the question why the Resolution of the Security Council to surrender the airport was not implemented. In May or June 1992 there was this Resolution banning all activities in the zone of the airport and along the access roads to Sarajevo. The BH Army at the time launched its Jug operation, which means south, and we know what the consequences were. That's why we insisted that this be implemented around the airport, namely, that the Resolution of the Security Council be implemented on the ground. About the -- about flights, both transport, or rather, freight planes are meant that brought any assets for UNPROFOR are meant as well as NATO aviation in the SRK zone of responsibility. In early 1992 there were already instances when the aviation flying over our positions, breaking the sound barrier causing dismay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't recorded that the General said flights bringing humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you mention humanitarian aid, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the main purpose of the airport and the reason why we handed over to UNPROFOR; namely, for humanitarian aid to be delivered to Sarajevo and materiel and technical equipment for UNPROFOR as well, including provisions and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3458, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you and how recommend to your subordinate commands what kind of relations they should have with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subordinate commands even before me received orders from commanders of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that they need to co-operate with UNPROFOR and what that co-operation included. When I arrived I issued orders of my own and I believe that they were clear and precise enough about that co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D06310.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at this. It is one of a number of warnings of yours. Let us look at paragraph 3 and paragraph 4. What are you here warning the commands?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean paragraphs 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I hereby warn all commands. You needn't read it out, just summarise it and tell us how often you sent out such warnings.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. This must have been about some problems with the relations with some UNPROFOR components in the area of the SRK. I especially singled out the Egyptian Battalion. It says here: "Egyptians and other Muslims must not be singled out in advance on any grounds." When I say "other Muslims," I meant such units that belonged to the UN contingent. In a civil conflict, a religious conflict, an ethnic conflict, clearly there is resistance toward anything that doesn't fit in the context. One reason for waging the war was religious strife or intolerance. There must have been some actions that were not in line with our orders about relations with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to add: "They are very" -- the translation reads "very insulted by our mistrust of them." I believe it should have been translated different.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are very susceptible to our distrust of them or sensitive, because it's very difficult to co-operate with someone you don't trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just on religious grounds; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you shouldn't be distrustful based on religion because people are always people and religion is merely an addition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3459, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 1D06326, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you shed some light on this. This is a month or a month and a half later on 23 November. You were giving instructions to your subordinate units about relations with UNPROFOR. In paragraph 4 we read instances of negative, unprofessional, uncivilised behaviour of individuals and so on, and even the Serbian population in certain areas. Were such instances the consequence of any orders given by authorities or what may have been the reason for civilian population behaving toward UNPROFOR in this manner?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we scroll down because I want to see who sent -- actually, I want to see the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a telegram because this is a different style, that's why it's phrased differently from a report or an order. Now that I'm thinking back to that time, I'm trying to remember why I wrote this. There must have been an order from the Main Staff, given the fact that it was sent out to so many recipients, and there must have been some problems in our zone. In the area of Hadzici, the transportation of humanitarian aid went along three axes through our corps' zone. From Pazarici through Hadzici towards Sarajevo was one axis, and they carried humanitarian aid for civilians in the zone of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. We know what the problems were at Tarcin with the Silos camp and the other 40 or so camps for Serbs in the zone of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. And now some women gathered there and wanted to take care of these problems in their own way. We took some measures which were not always adequate. They wanted the Silos cases to be investigated, so they laid down on the road and wouldn’t let the convoy for Sarajevo pass. And now what do you do about that? It's always a dilemma. Commanders of the Sarajevo sector went there, commanders from other levels tried to solve the problem. In a word, people who were able to make promises. Because if someone knows that their son is being mistreated or killed in a camp, they of course don't want to let a humanitarian convoy pass to bring food for the Muslim army and civilians, i.e. the 1st Corps of the BH Army. This is about the reaction of civilians and how they can create problems. I pointed this out because this happened repeatedly, not so very often but it was repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3460, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D06327.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this was issued three or four days after the previous one. This is your order. In the preamble it says there have been serious oversights in the behaviour of members of the VRS towards members of the UNPROFOR. What follows is your order. Under 3 it says: "Make sure that members of your unit are polite towards UNPROFOR members ..." and so on and so forth. Under 4 it says: "Immediately implement disciplinary measures including criminal liability for any transgressions against UNPROFOR ..." So something prompted you three days later after the warning to issue an order and to threaten punishment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that it is. There were cases. For example, convoys from Pancevo that went down Mount Trebevic and proceeded across Pale, they were stopped in Sokolac and other places. Everybody wanted to control those convoys. Everybody wanted to flex their muscle, and that's why I had to warn everybody that humanitarian convoys could not and should not be stopped because it was well-known who had the authority to stop them and how to co-operate with their escorts. Most of the escorts came from the Ukrainian Battalion contingent. They were very tolerant. However, I'm sure that there must have been problems that prompted me to issue an order to follow that warning or instruction that we saw previously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D3461.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your personal relationship with UNPROFOR commanders? What kind of personal relationships did you forge with them?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of our personal relationship, I tried to establish good, friendly relationships. I know that General Razek used to say that the other members of his staff did not really understand him, that he felt isolated. Whether intentionally or by chance, he said that he was a Christian. That's what he told me, but then when he testified against me I realised that he was of Muslim faith. But it doesn't really matter. I knew how to establish good relationships with everybody. I believe that I respected them as much as they wanted me to. I invited them to unofficial meetings. They invited me in turn. I know Soubirou invited me the most, but I never attended any unofficial meetings with them. It would always be somebody else from my command. I myself never found the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he left, he asked me to see him off but I had already been pensioned off. I was no longer in the Sarajevo region.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 17007, the last document today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure that she heard the document number correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 17007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Lieutenant-Colonel Mole, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mole was the head of the UNMOs as far as I can remember. It was very difficult to distinguish between UNMOs and UNPROFOR. For a while we thought that they were both the same. At that time I really did not know who they belonged to because they were all United Nations members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page, please. Do you remember that you received this letter from Lieutenant-Colonel Mole. In this letter he congratulates you on your promotion, he wishes you all the best, and he praises the co-operation that he had with you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that letter, of course. Whoever left, and let me remind you that mandate was a short-term mandate, whenever they left they would send me a thank you letter. Most of them came to see me personally before they left. Most of them were UNMOs. I don't want to comment upon the personal part of this letter. In any case, it was about our personal relationship between myself and Mole. But in any case what you see in the letter I believe is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page in Serbian. We don't need the following page in English because I don't think it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here he thanks you for your courtesy to himself and your continued kindness to the UNMOs. And he says that he trusts that you will persevere in your endeavours to keep them safe, especially if circumstances deteriorated. Irrespective of the fact that this letter is personal, how does this letter tally with your experience with regard to the relationship that you had forged with the representatives of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That experience, as I've already told you, was positive. I tried to maintain very honest co-operation with them and that's what I was hoping for. I wanted that co-operation to be mutually beneficial as well. If such co-operation is based on honesty and sincerity, I believe that it can also be full. Of course there were influences of various politics and at various trials those people behaved quite differently. I don't know why. In my view, my relationship with them was always friendly. It seems that they are embarrassed to admit that. I don't know why. Why should they be ashamed of such relationship? If anything was happening at the time, why didn't they tell me that I was a bad man, that I was a bad commander, that I didn't know how to do my job properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll adjourn today here. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, with your leave, a couple of comments for the transcript and I have a question for the Chamber. I'll start with my comments. I'll be very quick so that the English version is the same as the French version. Page 13.11, there's a typo. It's more numerous rather than less numerous. Page 32, line 11, we distinguished. Page 71, line 2, General Galic talked about commissions in plural and not in singular. And finally, page 97, line 16, shouldn't be: "I'm not sure," but it should be: "I am sure." And then my question, Your Honour, has your -- the Chamber decided about the questions raised by General Galic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are taking a look into the matter. I will leave it at that. And as to the return date I think we can have -- you can hear Mr. Galic's evidence on Thursday. I don't think Mr. Akashi's evidence continued until the end of Thursdays so that we can hear him. And at that time, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did you ask whether -- when you should return?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Asking who, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you aware of the scheduling -- trial scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about next week, I don't think that there would be anything until the 7th, if you're talking about that week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume on 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Noted down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In Courtroom I. The hearing is adjourned.
